pĕcūlātus (PEQVLATVS, Lex Apparit.,
I. v. in the foll. ), ūs, m. peculor.
I. Lit., an embezzlement of public money, peculation: “peculatus furtum publicum a pecore dictum, sicut et pecunia, eo quod antiqui Romani nihil praeter pecora habebant,” Fest. p. 212 Müll.: “perfidia et peculatus ex urbe si exulant,” Plaut. Pers. 4, 4, 7 ; Cic. Phil. 12, 5, 12: “peculatum facere,” id. Rab. Perd. 3, 8 : “accusari peculatus,” Auct. Her. 1, 12, 22 : “peculatus damnari,” Cic. Fl. 18, 43 ; Liv. 33, 47: “SINE MALO PEQVLATV, Lex Apparit. Grut. 628: judices qui peculatu provincias quassavissent, Cod. Th. 9, 28, 1: ad legem Juliam peculatus,” Dig. 48 , tit. 13.—
II. Transf., of the caprice of love: perfidiosus est Amor. Si. Ergo in me peculatum facit, Plaut. Cist. 1, 1, 73.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
